html:
The Indo-Parthian Kingdom was a state ruled by Parthian lords in what is now eastern Iran, southern Afghanistan and Pakistan, in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. The map calls it the "Suren Kingdom" after the House of Suren, the great Parthian noble family its rulers are thought to have come from, and shows it from the turn of the eras to 400 CE.

Around 19 CE Gondophares I, governor of Sistan for the Parthian Empire, made himself independent. He took Arachosia and Gandhara from the Indo-Scythians and Indo-Greeks, and ruled as far as Taxila. Indian texts called these people Pahlavas.

Gondophares is the king named in the Acts of Thomas, which say the apostle Thomas came to his court; that is how Christian tradition places Thomas in India. The Buddhist monastery of Takht-i-Bahi is linked to this period.

In the late 1st century the Kushans took most of their eastern lands. They held Sistan until the Sasanians conquered it around 224. The map's later snapshots keep the old label.
